x.ASV: A Psalm of David. Blessed be Jehovah my rock, Who teacheth my hands to war, And my fingers to fight:
x.Darby: [A Psalm] of David. Blessed be Jehovah my rock, who teacheth my hands to war, my fingers to fight;
x.KJV: A Psalm of David. Blessed be the Lord my strength, which teacheth my hands to war, and my fingers to fight:
x.YLT: By David. Blessed is Jehovah my rock, who is teaching My hands for war, my fingers for battle.

nt: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I bless Yahweh] or [Let me praise Yahweh]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a high **rock** that David could climb up to reach safety from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [my protector]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the one teaching my hands for war, the one training my fingers for battle]

x.ASV: My lovingkindness, and my fortress, My high tower, and my deliverer; My shield, and he in whom I take refuge; Who subdueth my people under me.
x.Darby: My mercy and my fortress, my high tower and my deliverer, my shield and he in whom I trust, who subdueth my people under me!
x.KJV: My goodness, and my fortress; my high tower, and my deliverer; my shield, and he in whom I trust; who subdueth my people under me.
x.YLT: My kind one, and my bulwark, My tower, and my deliverer, My shield, and in whom I have trusted, Who is subduing my people under me!

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who is faithfully committed to me by covenant]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **my fortress** and **my stronghold**, strong places where he could go for safety, and as if he were **my shield**, a defensive weapon that protects from attack. If these images communicate well in your language, please use them. If not, you could express them in a different way. Alternate translation: [and my protector, my safe place and the one rescuing me, my defender]

The terms **fortress** and **stronghold** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [my strong fortress]

David is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a place of **refuge** where he could go to hide from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [and in whom I find safety]

x.ASV: Jehovah, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him? Or the son of man, that thou makest account of him?
x.Darby: Jehovah, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him, the son of man, that thou takest thought of him?
x.KJV: Lord, what is man, that thou takest knowledge of him! or the son of man, that thou makest account of him!
x.YLT: Jehovah, what is man that Thou knowest him? Son of man, that Thou esteemest him?

nt: David is not asking for information about **man**. He is using the question form to emphasize how small and insignificant people are compared to God. If you would not use a rhetorical question for this purpose in your language, you could translate his words as a statement or an exclamation and communicate the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [people are so insignificant that you should not pay attention to them, and the son of man is not worth considering.]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [what is man, that you know him; indeed, what is the son of man, that you consider him]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what is a human being]
Although the term **son of man** is masculine, David is using the phrase in a generic sense that includes both men and women. Alternate translation: [the child of humanity] or [a human being]

x.ASV: Man is like to vanity: His days are as a shadow that passeth away.
x.Darby: Man is like to vanity; his days are as a shadow that passeth away.
x.KJV: Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away.
x.YLT: Man to vanity hath been like, His days are as a shadow passing by.

nt: David is speaking of **Man** as if he were **vapor**, something that appears briefly and then is gone. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [A person is like a puff of smoke]
Although the term **Man** is masculine, David is using the word in a generic sense that includes both men and women. Alternate translation: [A person]

David uses a comparison to express how quickly a person’s **days** pass. He says they are **like a passing shadow**, something that quickly moves and vanishes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his days pass quickly]

x.ASV: Bow thy heavens, O Jehovah, and come down: Touch the mountains, and they shall smoke.
x.Darby: Jehovah, bow thy heavens, and come down; touch the mountains, that they smoke;
x.KJV: Bow thy heavens, O Lord, and come down: touch the mountains, and they shall smoke.
x.YLT: Jehovah, incline Thy heavens and come down, Strike against mountains, and they smoke.

nt: These are imperatives, but they communicate polite requests rather than commands. Use forms in your language that communicate polite requests. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [please bow your heavens and come down]

The phrase **that they may smoke** communicates the purpose for which David asks God to touch the mountains. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that the second phrase describes the purpose for the first phrase. Alternate translation: [touch the mountains so that they smoke]

The psalmist is saying what he wants **Yahweh** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [please touch the mountains, that they may smoke]

x.ASV: Cast forth lightning, and scatter them; Send out thine arrows, and discomfit them.
x.Darby: Cast forth lightnings, and scatter them; send forth thine arrows, and discomfit them:
x.KJV: Cast forth lightning, and scatter them: shoot out thine arrows, and destroy them.
x.YLT: Send forth lightning, and scatter them, Send forth Thine arrows, and trouble them,

nt: בְּר֣וֹק בָּ֭רָק וּ⁠תְפִיצֵ֑⁠ם שְׁלַ֥ח חִ֝צֶּ֗י⁠ךָ וּ⁠תְהֻמֵּֽ⁠ם

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. It would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. However, if it would be unclear in your language, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Light lightning and scatter them; yes, send your arrows and rout them]

David is repeating forms of the word **lighten** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Flash your lightening]
The pronoun **them** refers to David’s enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [and scatter my enemies]

David is speaking of lightning bolts as if they were **arrows** that God shoots at his enemies. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [send your lightning bolts]

x.ASV: Stretch forth thy hand from above; Rescue me, and deliver me out of great waters, Out of the hand of aliens;
x.Darby: Stretch out thy hands from above; rescue me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of aliens,
x.KJV: Send thine hand from above; rid me, and deliver me out of great waters, from the hand of strange children;
x.YLT: Send forth Thy hand from on high, Free me, and deliver me from many waters, From the hand of sons of a stranger,

nt: Here, **hands** represents Yahweh’s power and action. David speaks of God acting on his behalf as if God were reaching out his **hands from above**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Use your power from above]

The phrases **break me free** and **deliver me** mean similar things. David is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deliver me to freedom]

David is speaking of his troubles as if they were **many waters** that could overwhelm him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from great troubles]

Here, **the hand** represents the power or control that the foreigners have. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of sons of a foreigner]

David is using the possessive form to describe **sons** or people who are characterized by being a **foreigner**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [foreigners]

x.ASV: Whose mouth speaketh deceit, And whose right hand is a right hand of falsehood.
x.Darby: Whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.
x.KJV: Whose mouth speaketh vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.
x.YLT: Because their mouth hath spoken vanity, And their right hand is a right hand of falsehood.

nt: Here, **their mouth** represents the foreigners themselves speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they speak worthlessness]
אֲשֶׁ֣ר פִּ֭י⁠הֶם דִּבֶּר־שָׁ֑וְא וִֽ֝⁠ימִינָ֗⁠ם יְמִ֣ין שָֽׁקֶר

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **worthlessness** and **falsehood**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [who, their mouth speaks what is worthless, and their right hand is a right hand of what is false]

Here, **their right hand** represents the oath that a person swears by raising the right hand. David says their oath is **a right hand of falsehood**, meaning they swear falsely. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they swear false oaths]

x.Darby: OGod, I will sing a new song unto thee; with the ten-stringed lute will I sing psalms unto thee:

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [who provides salvation] or [who grants deliverance]

David is speaking about himself in the third person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [me, David, your servant] or [me, who serves you]

Here, **the evil sword** represents violence and warfare. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from violent warfare]

x.ASV: When our sons shall be as plants grown up in their youth, And our daughters as corner-stones hewn after the fashion of a palace;
x.Darby: That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; our daughters as corner-columns, sculptured after the fashion of a palace:
x.KJV: That our sons may be as plants grown up in their youth; that our daughters may be as corner stones, polished after the similitude of a palace:
x.YLT: Because our sons are as plants, Becoming great in their youth, Our daughters as hewn stones, Polished--the likeness of a palace,

nt: The word **that** introduces the purpose for which David has been asking God to rescue him and his people. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows describes the purpose for the previous actions. Alternate translation: [so that our sons may be like plants]

Here David compares **sons** to **plants** that are well-established and growing. This means the sons are strong and healthy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our sons may be strong and healthy]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that grow large]

Here David compares **daughters** to **corner pillars** that are carved beautifully. This means the daughters are beautiful and strong. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent comparison or express this meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our daughters may be beautiful and strong]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that our daughters may be like corner pillars carved in the pattern of a palace]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that someone carved to decorate a palace]

x.ASV: When our garners are full, affording all manner of store, And our sheep bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our fields;
x.Darby: Our granaries full, affording all manner of store; our sheep bringing forth thousands, ten thousands in our pastures;
x.KJV: That our garners may be full, affording all manner of store: that our sheep may bring forth thousands and ten thousands in our streets:
x.YLT: Our garners are full, bringing out from kind to kind, Our flocks are bringing forth thousands, Ten thousands in our out-places,

nt: The implication is that the storehouses are full of many different **kind** of food. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express that explicitly. Alternate translation: [providing many different kinds of food]

In keeping with the conventions of his language, David is using the numbers “thousand” and “myriad” as verbs. He does not mean those exact numbers. He is using them to mean great quantities. Translate these numbers according to the conventions of your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [may our flocks multiply by the thousands and ten thousands in our fields] or [may our flocks multiply in very great numbers in our fields]

x.ASV: When our oxen are well laden; When there is no breaking in, and no going forth, And no outcry in our streets:
x.Darby: Our kine laden [with young]; no breaking in and no going forth, and no outcry in our streets.
x.KJV: That our oxen may be strong to labour; that there be no breaking in, nor going out; that there be no complaining in our streets.
x.YLT: Our oxen are carrying, there is no breach, And there is no outgoing, And there is no crying in our broad places.

nt: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May our oxen carry heavy burdens]

The implication is that there will be **no breach** in the city walls, **no going out** to war, and **no cry** of distress in the streets. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express that explicitly. Alternate translation: [no enemy breaks through our walls, and no one goes out to war, and no one cries of distress]

x.ASV: Happy is the people that is in such a case; Yea, happy is the people whose God is Jehovah.
x.Darby: Blessed the people that is in such a case! Blessed the people whoseGod is Jehovah!
x.KJV: Happy is that people, that is in such a case: yea, happy is that people, whose God is the Lord.
x.YLT: O the happiness of the people that is thus, O the happiness of the people whose God is Jehovah!

nt: David is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is the people for whom it is thus to it! How happy is]

Here, **it** refers back to **the people**, which is a singular noun which refers to a group. David is saying the people have the blessings he has just described. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the referent explicit. Alternate translation: [who has all of these blessings]

Here, **its** refers back to **the people**, which is a singular noun which refers to a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the referent explicit or use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [whose God is Yahweh]
